la:adj:sagax.gloss: of quick perception, having acute senses; keen-scented
senses: of quick perception, having acute senses; keen-scented
intellectually quick, keen, acute, shrewd, sagacious
la:adj:sagax.html:
săgax, ācis, adj.
sagio; cf. salax, from salio
,
of quick perception, whose senses are acute, sagacious (class.).
Lit.
Chiefly of the acute sense of smelling in dogs, keen-scented: sagax Nasum habet,: canes,; : catulus,. —With gen.: naris sagax,.— Poet.: virtus venandi,.—
Of other senses: sollicitive canes canibusve sagacior anser,: palatum in gustu sagacissimum,. —
Trop., intellectually quick, keen, acute, shrewd, sagacious (syn.: sollers, perspicax, acutus, subtilis).
Absol.: (homo) animal hoc providum, sagax, multiplex, acutum, memor, plenum rationis et consilii,; cf. : mens,; ; : animus,; : ratio,; : homo sagax et astutus,: modo circumspectus et sagax, modo inconsultus ac praeceps,considerate,: mire sagaces fallere hospites,: curae,.—Of a soothsayer, knowing the future, .—
Ad aliquid (class.): ad suspicandum sagacissimus,: ad haec pericula perspicienda, Plancus ap. .—
With gen. (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): utilium sagax rerum et divina futuri,: fibrarum et pennae divinarumque flammarum,skilled in,; cf. in sup.: prodigiorum (Joseph),; and: rerum naturae, Col. praef., § 22 (with non ignarus). —
With in or simple abl. (post-Aug.): vir in conjecturis sagacissimus,: civitas rimandis offensis sagax,.—(ρ) Inf.: sagax quondam ventura videre,.—Hence, adv.: să-gācĭter.
Quickly, sharply, keenly, with quickness of scent, with a fine sense of smell: canes si advenientem sagaciter odorantur,.—Comp., : vultures sagacius odorantur,; .—Sup., ; .—
Trop., acutely, shrewdly, accurately, sagaciously: sagaciter pervestigare,: intueri,; : perspicere naturam alicujus,

la:noun:sagacitas.html:
săgācĭtas, ātis, f.
sagax
,
keenness of perception, acuteness of the senses, sagacity.
Lit.
Keenness of scent in dogs: canum tam incredibilis ad investigandum sagacitas narium,; so, canum,.—*
Transf., of hunters: ut domitas feras mentita sagacitate colligerent,.—*
Keenness, acuteness of the other senses: sensuum,.—
Trop., intellectual keenness of perception, acuteness, shrewdness, sagacity (good prose; syn.: sollertia, acumen): utrum admonitus ac tentatus, an, quā est ipse sagacitate in his rebus, sine duce ullo, sine indice, pervenerit ad hanc improbitatem, nescio,: tuam tantam fuisse sagacitatem,, § 29: erat eā sagacitate, ut decipi non posset,: consilii,: Hipparchi sagacitate compertum est, lunae defectum, etc.,.

la:other:Saguntum.html:
Săguntum, i, n., and Săguntus (-os), i, f., = Σάγουντον,
a town in Hispania Tarraconensis, on the Mediterranean, beyond the Iberus, the besieging and reduction of which by Hannibal led to the breaking out of the second Punic war; now Murviedro.—Neutr., ; ; .—Fem., ; ; ; ; ; cf.: Graia Saguntos,.—Doubtful form, ; ; ; et saep. —Hence, Săguntīnus (Săguntĭus, ), a, um, adj., of or belonging to Saguntum, Saguntine: ficus,: id. ap. : lutum (from which utensils were made),; ; cf. lagena,: clades,: rabies,: ignis, et saep.—Subst., in plur.: Săguntīni, ōrum, m., the people of Saguntum, the Saguntines, ; sq.; Auct. B. Hisp. 8; .

la:noun:sagina.html:
săgīna, ae, f.
kindr. with σάττω, to stuff full, to cram; v. sagmen
,
a stuffing, cramming, fattening, feeding, feasting.
Lit.
In abstr. (class.): anserum,; ; : gallinarum,: cochlearum,: vaccarum. : dies noctesque estur, Bibitur, neque quisquam parsimoniam adhibet: sagina plane est,: in saginam se conicere,: qui multitudinem illam non auctoritate sed sagina tenebat, * ; cf. .—
In concr.
Food, nourishment (postAug.).
Lit.: gladiatoria sagina,; cf., of gladiators' food,temulentus et sagina gravis,: stomachum laxare saginae,: sagina viva,i. e. small fish with which larger ones were fed,; cf. : ad saginam idonea,: ferarum,: minuere saginam,: ad saginam pristinam revocare,to natural food,: bestiarum,.—
Transf.: herbae viridis coma dulciore saginā roris aut fluminis,rich nourishment, Mai: quemadmodum forensibus certaminibus exercitatos et quasi militantes reficit ac reparat haec velut sagina dicendi,nourishment of oratory,.—*
A fatted animal: este, effercite vos, saginam caedite,kill the fatted beast,.—
Meton., fatness produced by much eating, corpulence (postAug.): saginam corporis ex nimiā luxuriā contraxit,: sagina ventris non homini sed beluae similis,: qui colorem fuco et verum robur inani saginā mentiuntur,: nimio tendis mole saginam,: ursam quae ceteris saginā corporis praevalebat,.

la:verb:sagino.html:
săgīno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
sagina
(class.; cf. educare).
Lit.
Of animals, to fatten, fat: pullos columbinos,: boves ad sacrificia,: aves offis,: equum hordeo ervoque (with roborare largo cibo),: porcum,: corpus,: glires fagi glande,: catulos ferarum molliore praedā, et saep.—
Of persons, to cram, stuff, feast: saginare plebem populares suos, ut jugulentur,: nuptialibus cenis,: terra, quae copiā rerum omnium (illos Gallos) saginaret,: cum exquisitis cottidie Antonius saginaretur epulis,: convivas,.—
Transf., to feed, nourish, etc.: terra multorum annorum frondibus et herbis, velut saginata largioribus pabulis,; : fons umore supero saginatus,: qui ab illo pestifero ac perdito cive jampridem rei publicae sanguine saginantur, * ; ; .—Hence, săgīnātus, a, um, P. a., fattened, fat (late Lat.): saginatior hostia,; so, Christianus ursis,: vitulum,.

A bawd, procuress: sagae mulieres dicuntur feminae ad libidinem virorum indagatrices,: ut saga et bona conciliatrix, Lucil. ap. : saga conducta pretio,.

la:noun:sagum.html:
săgum, i, n. (ante-class. collat. form săgus, i, m., corresp. to the Greek, Enn. and Varr. ap. ; Afran. ap. P.;
fem.: sagas caerulas, Enn. ap. P.; but it would perh. be more correct to read sagos caerulos; cf. Vahl.), = σάγος [acc. to Polybius, a Celtic word, whence the Engl. shag], a coarse woollen blanket or mantle (cf. laena), e. g. of servants, ; ; ; of the Germans,; for horses,, 4; 3, 15, 16; but most freq. of soldiers, a military cloak: valde metuo ne frigeas in hibernis ... praesertim qui sagis non abundares,; ; : saga fibulatoria,.—Hence, saga is a sign of war (as toga is a sign of peace) in the phrases:
Saga sumere, to put on the saga, i.q. to take up arms, prepare for battle (it was the custom for all Romans to do this, in token of preparation for war, even those who were not going to the field, excepting persons of consular rank; cf. ; id. Fragm. ap. ): tumultum decerni, justitium edici, saga sumi dico oportere, delectum habere, etc.,; ; : terrā marique victus hostis punico Lugubre mutavit sagum,; in sing., of an individual: tum iste (Verres) excitatus sagum sumit,.—
In the same signif.: ad saga ire,; cf. .—
In sagis esse, to be under arms: cum est in sagis civitas,.—
Saga ponere, to lay down one's arms, .—
In gen. (eccl. Lat.), a covering.
A curtain, tent-cover, ; , etc.—
A garment, .
